cards.question: What does "PThreads" stand for?
cards.answer: POSIX Threads
cards.memory: The de facto thread standard on UNIX systems.

cards.question: What does POSIX stand for?
cards.answer: Portable Operating System Interface
cards.memory: "Portable" = its goal is interoperability across OSes.

cards.question: What is the goal of the POSIX standard?
cards.answer: Define a common system-call interface so programs are portable across OSes.
distractors: Define a standard for CPU instruction sets.
Make threads run faster on Linux only.

cards.question: What PThreads data type represents a thread?
cards.answer: pthread_t

cards.question: What does a pthread_t hold?
cards.answer: The thread's ID, execution state, and other info (mostly managed by the library).
distractors: The thread's full address space and page table.

cards.question: Birrell's fork ≈ which PThreads call?
cards.answer: pthread_create()

cards.question: Birrell's join ≈ which PThreads call?
cards.answer: pthread_join()

cards.question: pthread_create(____, attr, start_routine, arg) — what is the first argument?
cards.answer: A pointer to the pthread_t that will be filled in for the new thread.
distractors: The start routine the thread will run.
The argument passed to the start routine.

cards.question: What does pthread_create() return?
cards.answer: A status code: success or failure.
distractors: The new thread's ID as an int.

cards.question: What two arguments does pthread_join() take?
cards.answer: The thread to join and a pointer to receive its return status/result.
distractors: The start routine and its argument.
The thread and an attribute structure.

cards.question: What does passing NULL as the attr argument to pthread_create() do?
cards.answer: Uses PThreads' default attributes.
distractors: Makes the thread inherit no stack.

cards.question: Name 3 things you can set with pthread_attr_t.
cards.answer: Any 3 of: stack size, scheduling policy/priority, scope, inheritance, joinable/detached.
distractors: Mutex type, CV type, and signal handler.
Page size, heap size, and file limit.
Program counter, stack pointer, and registers.

cards.question: Which calls create and free a pthread_attr_t?
cards.answer: pthread_attr_init() / pthread_attr_destroy()

cards.question: Which calls read or change a single thread attribute?
cards.answer: pthread_attr_set*() / pthread_attr_get*() (e.g., pthread_attr_setdetachstate)

cards.question: By default, are PThreads joinable or detached?
cards.answer: Joinable
distractors: Joinable only if created by main

cards.question: What can happen if a parent thread exits before joining its joinable children?
cards.answer: The children can become zombies (finished, but never reaped).
cards.memory: Joinable = the parent must stay and "pick up" its kids.
distractors: The children take over as the new parent.

cards.question: What is a detached thread?
cards.answer: A thread that cannot be joined; it keeps running even if its parent exits.
cards.memory: Detached = the kid has moved out. No one waits for it.
distractors: A thread that runs in its own process.
A thread that can't be preempted.
A thread whose parent must join it.

cards.question: Which PThreads mechanism is NOT in Birrell's model?
cards.answer: Detached threads

cards.question: How do you detach an already-created thread?
cards.answer: pthread_detach(thread)

cards.question: What attribute value makes a thread start out detached?
cards.answer: PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED (set via pthread_attr_setdetachstate)

cards.question: How does a parent of detached threads exit without killing them?
cards.answer: It calls pthread_exit().

cards.question: What does PTHREAD_SCOPE_SYSTEM scope mean for a new thread?
cards.answer: It competes equally for CPU with every other thread in the system.
distractors: It competes only with threads in the same process.
It runs only on one CPU.
It has higher priority than all other threads.

cards.question: Which header must a PThreads program include?
cards.answer: pthread.h

cards.question: Which compiler flag links the PThreads library?
cards.answer: -lpthread (or, better on some platforms, -pthread)
cards.memory: -pthread = link the library AND configure compilation for threads.

cards.question: What happens if you forget to link the PThreads library?
cards.answer: Some errors may not show at compile time, but the program still fails.
distractors: The compiler always reports a clear error.
The program runs single-threaded but correctly.

cards.question: In Example 1, 4 threads each run hello() (prints "Hello Thread"). What is the output?
cards.answer: "Hello Thread" printed 4 times.
distractors: Output is undefined; it may print 0 to 4 times.

cards.question: Why might threads print in a different order than they were created?
cards.answer: The scheduler, not creation order, decides when each thread runs.
distractors: Threads always run in reverse creation order.

cards.question: In Example 2, the loop passes &i to each thread. Why can "Thread number 1" go missing?
cards.answer: main incremented the shared i before thread 1 read it, so two threads saw i = 2.
cards.memory: Every thread gets the SAME address → they see whatever i is at read time.

cards.question: What is a data race (race condition)?
cards.answer: One thread reads a variable while another thread is modifying it.
distractors: Two threads competing to finish first.
A thread running faster than the scheduler.
Two threads waiting on each other's locks.

cards.question: How was the Example 2 race on i fixed?
cards.answer: Copy i into tNum[i] and pass &tNum[i], giving each thread its own private copy.
cards.memory: Rule: never pass the address of a loop variable to a thread.
distractors: Lock a mutex around the printf.
Declare i as a global variable.

cards.question: What PThreads type represents a mutex?
cards.answer: pthread_mutex_t

cards.question: How does PThreads lock differ from Birrell's lock block?
cards.answer: PThreads uses explicit pthread_mutex_lock()/unlock() calls, not a { } block.
cards.memory:
Birrell: Lock(m) { ... } — the braces unlock for you.
PThreads: lock(); ...; unlock(); — you must unlock yourself.
distractors: PThreads unlocks automatically at the end of the block.
PThreads has no unlock; the lock expires.

cards.question: What must you do before using a pthread_mutex_t?
cards.answer: Initialize it: pthread_mutex_init() or PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER.
distractors: Nothing; mutexes are ready to use when declared.
Lock it once to activate it.

cards.question: By default, can a PThreads mutex be shared between processes?
cards.answer: No. It is private to one process unless you set the attribute to share it.
distractors: Yes. All mutexes are system-wide by default.

cards.question: How does pthread_mutex_trylock() differ from pthread_mutex_lock()?
cards.answer: If the mutex is taken, trylock returns immediately instead of blocking.
cards.memory: trylock = knock on the door; don't wait on the porch.
distractors: trylock spins until the mutex is free.
trylock gives the mutex to the longest waiter.
trylock locks two mutexes at once.

cards.question: Which call frees a mutex when you're done?
cards.answer: pthread_mutex_destroy()

cards.question: Where must mutexes be declared so every thread can see them?
cards.answer: As global variables.
distractors: As local variables in each thread function.

cards.question: How do you prevent deadlock when a thread needs several mutexes?
cards.answer: All threads lock the mutexes in the same global order.
distractors: Each thread uses its own mutex.

cards.question: Why is a forgotten unlock so easy to miss with PThreads?
cards.answer: Lock and unlock are separate calls, and the compiler won't warn you.
distractors: The compiler inserts unlocks for you.
The OS unlocks after a timeout.

cards.question: What PThreads type represents a condition variable?
cards.answer: pthread_cond_t

cards.question: What two arguments does pthread_cond_wait() take?
cards.answer: The condition variable and its mutex.
distractors: The thread ID and the mutex.

cards.question: What does pthread_cond_wait() do to the mutex?
cards.answer: Releases it while waiting and reacquires it before returning.
cards.memory: Same semantics as Birrell's Wait(m, c).
distractors: Holds it the whole time it waits.
Releases it and doesn't reacquire it.

cards.question: pthread_cond_signal() vs pthread_cond_broadcast()?
cards.answer: signal wakes one waiting thread; broadcast wakes all of them.
distractors: signal wakes all; broadcast wakes one.
signal is for processes; broadcast is for threads.

cards.question: Unsure whether to signal or broadcast? What's the safe default?
cards.answer: broadcast (it is correct, but slower).

cards.question: Which calls create and free a condition variable?
cards.answer: pthread_cond_init() / pthread_cond_destroy()

cards.question: Why might you signal/broadcast AFTER unlocking the mutex?
cards.answer: Signaling doesn't need the mutex, and it avoids spurious wake-ups.
distractors: Signaling requires the mutex to be free.
It makes the waiting thread skip the while check.
It avoids deadlock in all cases.

cards.question: Producer/consumer: what do num, add, and rem track in the shared buffer?
cards.answer: num = item count; add = next slot to write; rem = next slot to read.
distractors: num = buffer size; add = producer count; rem = consumer count.
num = next slot to read; add = count; rem = next slot to write.
num = threads waiting; add = items added total; rem = items removed total.

cards.question: Producer/consumer: when does the producer wait, and on which CV?
cards.answer: When num == BUFFER_SIZE (buffer full); it waits on c_prod.
distractors: When num == 0; it waits on c_cons.
When num == BUFFER_SIZE; it waits on c_cons.
When num == 0; it waits on c_prod.

cards.question: Producer/consumer: when does the consumer wait, and on which CV?
cards.answer: When num == 0 (buffer empty); it waits on c_cons.
distractors: When num == BUFFER_SIZE; it waits on c_prod.
When num == 0; it waits on c_prod.
When num == BUFFER_SIZE; it waits on c_cons.

cards.question: Why does the producer use signal (not broadcast) after adding an item?
cards.answer: Only one item was added, so only one consumer can make progress.
distractors: Broadcast would wake the producer too.

cards.question: How do add and rem wrap around the fixed-size buffer?
cards.answer: Modulo: add = (add + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE
distractors: They reset to 0 when the buffer is empty.
They're decremented back to 0 each time.
